        <script>
          document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", function () {
            function typeset(el) {
              if (window.MathJax && MathJax.typesetPromise) { MathJax.typesetPromise([el]).catch(function () {}); }
            }
            function makeButton(text, cls) {
              var b = document.createElement("button");
              b.type = "button"; b.textContent = text; if (cls) b.className = cls;
              return b;
            }

            /* ---- Collapsible, colour-coded sections (closed at first) ---- */
            var sections = Array.prototype.slice.call(document.querySelectorAll("main section.level2"));
            function setOpen(sec, open) {
              sec.classList.toggle("se-collapsed", !open);
              var h = sec.querySelector(":scope > .se-sec-head h2");
              if (h) h.setAttribute("aria-expanded", String(open));
              if (open) typeset(sec);
            }
            sections.forEach(function (sec) {
              var h = sec.querySelector(":scope > h2");
              if (!h) return;
              var classes = Array.prototype.slice.call(sec.classList).concat(Array.prototype.slice.call(h.classList));
              var theme = classes.filter(function (c) { return c.indexOf("se-theme-") === 0; })[0];
              if (theme) {
                sec.classList.add(theme);
                if (sec.id) {
                  var tocLink = document.querySelector('#TOC a[href="#' + sec.id + '"]');
                  if (tocLink) tocLink.classList.add(theme, "se-toc-themed");
                }
              }
              var head = document.createElement("div"); head.className = "se-sec-head";
              var body = document.createElement("div"); body.className = "se-sec-body";
              sec.insertBefore(head, h);
              head.appendChild(h);
              Array.prototype.slice.call(sec.childNodes).forEach(function (n) { if (n !== head) body.appendChild(n); });
              sec.appendChild(body);
              var chev = document.createElement("span"); chev.className = "se-chev"; chev.textContent = "▾";
              h.appendChild(chev);
              h.setAttribute("role", "button"); h.tabIndex = 0;
              head.addEventListener("click", function (e) {
                if (e.target.closest("a")) return;
                setOpen(sec, sec.classList.contains("se-collapsed"));
              });
              h.addEventListener("keydown", function (e) {
                if (e.key === "Enter" || e.key === " ") { e.preventDefault(); setOpen(sec, sec.classList.contains("se-collapsed")); }
              });
              setOpen(sec, false);
            });
            if (sections.length) {
              var ctl = document.createElement("div"); ctl.className = "se-sec-controls";
              var expandAll = makeButton("Expand all"), collapseAll = makeButton("Collapse all");
              expandAll.addEventListener("click", function () { sections.forEach(function (s) { setOpen(s, true); }); });
              collapseAll.addEventListener("click", function () { sections.forEach(function (s) { setOpen(s, false); }); });
              ctl.appendChild(expandAll); ctl.appendChild(collapseAll);
              sections[0].parentNode.insertBefore(ctl, sections[0]);
            }
            function openFor(id) {
              if (!id) return;
              var t = document.getElementById(id);
              var sec = t && t.closest("section.level2");
              if (sec) setOpen(sec, true);
            }
            document.addEventListener("click", function (e) {
              var a = e.target.closest('a[href^="#"]');
              if (a) openFor(decodeURIComponent(a.getAttribute("href").slice(1)));
            });
            window.addEventListener("hashchange", function () { openFor(decodeURIComponent(location.hash.slice(1))); });
            if (location.hash) openFor(decodeURIComponent(location.hash.slice(1)));

            /* ---- Questions: wrong answers struck out, right answer reveals feedback, running score ---- */
            var quizzes = document.querySelectorAll(".se-quiz");
            var scoreEls = document.querySelectorAll(".se-score");
            var score = 0, done = 0;
            function updateScore() {
              scoreEls.forEach(function (el) {
                el.textContent = "Correct first time: " + score + " / " + quizzes.length +
                  (done === quizzes.length ? "  — all done!" : "");
              });
            }
            quizzes.forEach(function (quiz) {
              var firstTry = true;
              quiz.querySelectorAll("span.se-option").forEach(function (span) {
                var btn = makeButton("", "se-option");
                btn.innerHTML = span.innerHTML;
                if (span.dataset.correct === "true") btn.dataset.correct = "true";
                span.replaceWith(btn);
                btn.addEventListener("click", function () {
                  if (quiz.classList.contains("solved")) return;
                  if (btn.dataset.correct === "true") {
                    btn.classList.add("right");
                    quiz.classList.add("solved");
                    quiz.querySelectorAll("button.se-option").forEach(function (b) { b.disabled = true; });
                    if (firstTry) score++;
                    done++;
                    updateScore();
                    typeset(quiz);
                  } else {
                    firstTry = false;
                    btn.classList.add("wrong");
                    btn.disabled = true;
                  }
                });
              });
            });
            updateScore();

            /* ---- Ask yourself: reveal the answer ---- */
            document.querySelectorAll(".se-precheck").forEach(function (box) {
              var reveal = box.querySelector(".se-reveal");
              if (!reveal) return;
              var label = reveal.dataset.label || "Check";
              var b = makeButton(label, "se-reveal-btn");
              box.insertBefore(b, reveal);
              b.addEventListener("click", function () {
                var open = reveal.classList.toggle("open");
                b.textContent = open ? "Hide" : label;
                if (open) typeset(reveal);
              });
            });

            /* ---- Dictionary: say the meaning, then reveal it ---- */
            var flips = [];
            document.querySelectorAll("span.se-flip").forEach(function (span) {
              var wrap = document.createElement("span");
              var btn = makeButton("Reveal", "se-flip");
              var shown = document.createElement("span"); shown.className = "se-flip-shown"; shown.hidden = true;
              shown.innerHTML = span.innerHTML;
              var hide = makeButton("hide", "se-hide"); shown.appendChild(hide);
              wrap.appendChild(btn); wrap.appendChild(shown);
              span.replaceWith(wrap);
              function set(open) { btn.hidden = open; shown.hidden = !open; if (open) typeset(shown); }
              btn.addEventListener("click", function () { set(true); });
              hide.addEventListener("click", function () { set(false); });
              flips.push(set);
            });
            document.querySelectorAll(".se-dict-controls").forEach(function (box) {
              var all = makeButton("Reveal all", "se-reveal-btn"), none = makeButton("Hide all", "se-reveal-btn");
              all.addEventListener("click", function () { flips.forEach(function (f) { f(true); }); });
              none.addEventListener("click", function () { flips.forEach(function (f) { f(false); }); });
              box.appendChild(all); box.appendChild(none);
            });
          });
        </script>
---

There are lots of different ways of writing maths that are equivalent and can be used interchangeably. This can be confusing if your lecturer uses a different notation than you are used to.

The reason that there are different ways to say the same thing in maths is because mathematical notation has been developed over many thousands of years by many different people.

In English 'big' (from Middle English) and 'large' (from Latin) mean the same thing. There are similar examples in maths.

::: {.se-box}
**The most important thing to remember** is that choice of notation is often cultural or simply personal preference, and therefore it is okay to ask for clarification.
:::

::: {.se-box .se-precheck}
::: {.se-prompt}
how many ways do I know of writing "$a$ multiplied by $b$"? Write them down before you open the first section.
:::
::: {.se-reveal data-label="Compare"}
$a \times b = a \cdot b = ab = a(b) = (a)b = (a)(b)$
:::
:::

## Numbers and calculations {.se-theme-teal}

### Division and multiplication

Sometimes we think of $\frac{a}{b}$ as a 'fraction' and $a\div b$ as a 'calculation', but they are actually interchangeable.

$$
\frac{2}{5} = 2\div 5 = 2/5
$$

When working with numbers we often use a multiplication sign $\times$, but this is usually dropped when working algebraically as it looks a bit like the letter $x$.

If you are working with vectors then it is important to distinguish between the cross product $a \times b$ and the dot product $a \cdot b$, but with scalars (e.g. straightforward numbers), they are interchangeable.

$$
a \times b = a \cdot b = ab = a(b) = (a)b = (a)(b)
$$

::: {.se-quiz}
Which of these is **not** another way of writing $\frac{7}{3}$?

[$7 \div 3$]{.se-option} [$7/3$]{.se-option} [$3 \div 7$]{.se-option data-correct="true"} [$\tfrac{7}{3}$]{.se-option}

::: {.se-feedback}
$3 \div 7 = \frac{3}{7}$. The order matters: the number written first (or on top) is the one being divided.
:::
:::

### Dots and commas

Different cultures tend to use dots and commas in different ways. If you aren't sure, please just ask your lecturer to clarify their notation.

A decimal point may be shown in several ways:

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
2 \frac{3}{10} & = 2 \cdot 3 \\
& = 2.3 \\
& = 2,3
\end{array}
$$

but a dot can also be used as multiplication

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
2 \times 3 & = 2 \cdot 3 \\
& = 2.3 \\
& = 2(3)
\end{array}
$$

Commas and dots might also be used for separating groups of a thousand

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
2145600 & = 2\ 145\ 600 \\
& = 2,145,600 \\
& = 2.145.600
\end{array}
$$

::: {.se-quiz}
Your lecturer writes $4 \cdot 5$ on the board. What does it mean?

[It is definitely $4.5$]{.se-option} [It is definitely $20$]{.se-option} [It could be either; check the context or ask]{.se-option data-correct="true"}

::: {.se-feedback}
A raised dot can be a decimal point or a multiplication sign. Look at how it is used elsewhere in the lecture, and if you are still unsure, ask.
:::
:::

::: {.se-box .se-precheck}
::: {.se-prompt}
what number is $1.000$?
:::
::: {.se-reveal data-label="Check"}
To most people in the UK $1.000$ is "one". In much of Europe it would be read as "one thousand". This is why it is worth asking when you aren't sure.
:::
:::

## Calculus {.se-theme-blue}

### Maths grammar

| Word | Part of speech | Meaning |
|:------|:-----|:----------------------------|
| Calculus | noun | The branch of maths that includes differentiation |
| Differentiation | noun | The process of finding the derivative |
| Differential | noun | The change in the variable; the differential of $x$ is $dx$ |
| Derivative | noun | $\frac{dy}{dx}$ = the rate of change of the function |
| Differentiate | verb | The act of finding the derivative; you differentiate the function $y$ to find $\frac{dy}{dx}$ |
| Derive | verb | Red herring! Whilst this sounds like the verb form of derivative it isn't! Use 'differentiate' instead. |

::: {.se-quiz}
Choose the correct word: "To find the gradient, we need to ______ $y = 3x^2$."

[derive]{.se-option} [differentiate]{.se-option data-correct="true"} [differential]{.se-option} [derivative]{.se-option}

::: {.se-feedback}
'Differentiate' is the verb. 'Derive' is the red herring: it sounds right but means something different.
:::
:::

### Equivalent ways of showing differentiation

Each column below shows the same idea written in a different notation.

$$
\begin{array}{llllllll}
\textbf{function} & f(x)= x^2 & y= x^2 & y = x^2 & u^2 & v = z^2 & s = t^2 & f(x) = x^2 \\
 & \color{orange}{\downarrow} & \color{blue}{\downarrow} & \color{green}{\downarrow} & \color{red}{\downarrow} & \color{purple}{\downarrow} & \color{olive}{\downarrow} & \color{magenta}{\downarrow} \\
\textbf{derivative} & f'(x)= 2x & \frac{dy}{dx}=2x & y' = 2x & \frac{d(u^2)}{du}=2u & \frac{d}{dz}v = 2z & \dot{s} = 2t & D(f) = 2x \\
 & \color{orange}{\downarrow} & \color{blue}{\downarrow} & \color{green}{\downarrow} & \color{red}{\downarrow} & \color{purple}{\downarrow} & \color{olive}{\downarrow} & \color{magenta}{\downarrow}\\
\textbf{second derivative} & f''(x) = 2 & \frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=2 & y'' = 2 & \frac{d^2(u^2)}{du^2}=2 & \frac{d^2}{dz^2}v = 2 & \ddot{s} = 2 & D^2(f) = 2
\end{array}
$$

::: {.se-quiz}
If $s = t^3$, which of these is the second derivative written in the same notation as the $\color{olive}{\text{olive}}$ column?

[$s'' = 6t$]{.se-option} [$\ddot{s} = 6t$]{.se-option data-correct="true"} [$\dot{s} = 3t^2$]{.se-option} [$D^2(s) = 6t$]{.se-option}

::: {.se-feedback}
Dot notation: one dot for the first derivative, two dots for the second. The other options are also correct values, but written in different notations; $\dot{s} = 3t^2$ is the first derivative.
:::
:::

::: {.se-box .se-precheck}
::: {.se-prompt}
which notation for differentiation did I use most at school or college? Which ones in the table are new to me?
:::
::: {.se-reveal data-label="Check"}
If any are new, try rewriting $\frac{dy}{dx} = 2x$ from the table in each of the other notations.
:::
:::

### Letters that look like d but mean different things

| Symbol | Said as | Meaning |
|:-----:|:----------|:----------------------|
| $\Delta x$ | "delta x" | the change in $x$ |
| $\delta x$ | "delta x" | the small change in $x$ |
| $dx$ | "the differential" | the change in $x$ when it approaches zero |
| $\partial x$ | "the partial differential" | the change in $x$ when it approaches zero |
| $d(x,y)$ | "distance between x and y" | the distance function (metric spaces and topology) |

::: {.se-quiz}
Which symbol means "the small change in $x$"?

[$\Delta x$]{.se-option} [$\delta x$]{.se-option data-correct="true"} [$\partial x$]{.se-option} [$d(x,y)$]{.se-option}

::: {.se-feedback}
Lowercase delta, $\delta x$, is the small change. Uppercase delta, $\Delta x$, is the change in $x$. Both are said "delta x", so watch the letter carefully.
:::
:::

## Exponentials {.se-theme-purple}

In the expression $a^b$, $b$ can be called the 'power', the 'exponent' or the 'index' (indices is the plural of index).

In the expression $e^b$, $e$ is a number that might be called 'Euler's number' (which is pronounced 'oy-luh').

The expression $e^x$ is a function, and can also be written in function notation:

$$
e^x = \exp(x) = \exp x
$$

The choice of notation might be used to emphasise that it is a function, or perhaps just to make it easier to read:

$$
e^{\frac{2x^2}{3 - x}} = \exp\left(\frac{2x^2}{3 - x}\right)
$$

::: {.se-quiz}
In $2^5$, what is the 5 **not** called?

[the power]{.se-option} [the exponent]{.se-option} [the index]{.se-option} [the base]{.se-option data-correct="true"}

::: {.se-feedback}
'Power', 'exponent' and 'index' all mean the same thing. The 2 is the base.
:::
:::

## Vectors {.se-theme-orange}

There are so many different notations that can be used for vectors, it can be very confusing.

Vectors are often written in lowercase, and vertices are often uppercase.

You can use a single letter to show a vector, or split it into its components.

$$
\begin{array}{lllll}
\overrightarrow{OA} & = \mathbf{a} & = \underset{\sim}{a} & = \vec{a} & = \underline{a}\\
= (a_1, a_2) & = (a_1 \ \ a_2) & = \begin{pmatrix} a_1 \\ a_2 \end{pmatrix} & = \begin{bmatrix} a_1 \\ a_2 \end{bmatrix} &\\
= a_1 \mathbf{i} + a_2 \mathbf{j} & = a_1 \hat{i} + a_2 \hat{j} & & &
\end{array}
$$

$\hat{a}$ is usually reserved for the 'unit vector in the direction of $\vec{a}$'.

::: {.se-box}
**Watch out for pointy brackets** though, as they are not used to show something is a vector, but for an operation involving two vectors (the inner product).

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\mathbf{a} = (a_1,a_2), \quad \mathbf{b} = (b_1,b_2) & \text{are vectors}\\
\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle & \text{is the inner product of the two vectors}
\end{array}
$$
:::

::: {.se-quiz}
Which of these is **not** a way of writing a vector?

[$\underline{a}$]{.se-option} [$\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}$]{.se-option} [$\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle$]{.se-option data-correct="true"} [$3\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j}$]{.se-option}

::: {.se-feedback}
Pointy brackets show the inner product of two vectors, not a vector itself.
:::
:::

## Matrices {.se-theme-pink}

Matrices are usually named with a letter, which is written in bold font. You can use curved or square brackets for a matrix, or sometimes even no bracket at all.

Another word for (curved) brackets is 'parentheses' and {curly} brackets are sometimes called 'braces'.

$$
\mathbf{A} =
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 2 & 3 \\
4 & 5 & 6 \\
7 & 8 & 9
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 2 & 3 \\
4 & 5 & 6 \\
7 & 8 & 9
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{matrix}
1 & 2 & 3 \\
4 & 5 & 6 \\
7 & 8 & 9
\end{matrix}
$$

As a general rule matrices are written with uppercase letters, $A$, and elements of a matrix are denoted with lowercase $a$. Each element of the matrix can be written with a subscript, $a_{ij}$, that tells you where it is located:

$$
\mathbf{A} =
\begin{pmatrix}
a_{1,1} & a_{1,2} \\
a_{2,1} & a_{2,2}
\end{pmatrix}
$$

Curly brackets are not generally used for matrices, but because they are used for set notation you could write a matrix using curly brackets:

$$
\mathbf{A} = \{a_{ij}\}
$$

::: {.se-quiz}
In the matrix $\mathbf{A}$ at the top of this section, what is $a_{2,3}$?

[$8$]{.se-option} [$6$]{.se-option data-correct="true"} [$2$]{.se-option} [$3$]{.se-option}

::: {.se-feedback}
The first subscript is the row and the second is the column: row 2, column 3 gives $6$.
:::
:::

### Straight lines

Straight vertical lines are used for a property of the matrix, rather than the matrix itself.

::: {.se-box}
**Watch out:** some lecturers' handwriting makes it tricky to tell what style of line is intended! If in doubt, just ask for clarification.
:::

Single lines show the determinant of a matrix (telling you something about the scale factor when using the matrix to enlarge a vector).

$$
\det(\mathbf{A}) =
\begin{vmatrix}
1 & 2 & 3 \\
4 & 5 & 6 \\
7 & 8 & 9
\end{vmatrix}
\ne
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 2 & 3 \\
4 & 5 & 6 \\
7 & 8 & 9
\end{pmatrix}
$$

Double lines are for the norm of a matrix (telling you something about the size of the elements).

$$
\operatorname{norm}(\mathbf{A}) =
\begin{Vmatrix}
1 & 2 & 3 \\
4 & 5 & 6 \\
7 & 8 & 9
\end{Vmatrix}
\ne
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 2 & 3 \\
4 & 5 & 6 \\
7 & 8 & 9
\end{pmatrix}
$$

If you are working with numbers or vectors then single and double lines are often used interchangeably to mean 'distance from the origin' or 'magnitude of the vector'.

$$
\begin{gathered}
\Vert -3 \Vert = \vert -3 \vert = \operatorname{abs}(-3) = 3 \\
\Vert (3,4) \Vert = \vert (3,4) \vert = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5
\end{gathered}
$$

::: {.se-quiz}
What is $\vert (6,8) \vert$?

[$14$]{.se-option} [$10$]{.se-option data-correct="true"} [$48$]{.se-option} [$\begin{pmatrix} 6 \\ 8 \end{pmatrix}$]{.se-option}

::: {.se-feedback}
For a vector, the straight lines mean its magnitude: $\sqrt{6^2 + 8^2} = \sqrt{100} = 10$.
:::
:::

## Statistics {.se-theme-gold}

### Random variables

In general uppercase letters are used to name random variables and lowercase letters are for the values of those variables.

For example:

| Notation | Meaning |
|:---------------:|:----------------------|
| $X$ | possible values obtained when rolling a dice |
| $x$ | the value after a single roll |
| $X = \{x\} = \{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$ | the set of possible values |
| $x_1, x_2, x_3$ | the results obtained from three rolls of the dice |
| $x_i$ | the value of one of the rolls of the dice |
| $P(X = x)$ | the probability that the value rolled is a specific value |
| $P(X = 2)$ | the probability that a 2 is rolled |

### Summary statistics

| Symbol | Said as | Meaning |
|:-----:|:----------|:----------------------|
| $\mu$ | 'mew' | population mean |
| $\mu_X$ | 'mew X' | population mean of $X$ |
| $\bar{x}$ | 'x bar' | sample mean |
| $\sigma$ | 'sigma' | standard deviation |
| $\sigma_X$ | 'sigma X' | standard deviation of $X$ |
| $s$ | | sample standard deviation |
| $\rho$ | 'ro' | product moment correlation coefficient of population |
| $r_x$ | | product moment correlation coefficient of sample |

::: {.se-quiz}
You collect the heights of 30 students and work out their average. Which symbol should you use?

[$\mu$]{.se-option} [$\bar{x}$]{.se-option data-correct="true"} [$\sigma$]{.se-option} [$X$]{.se-option}

::: {.se-feedback}
The 30 students are a sample, so their average is the sample mean, $\bar{x}$. $\mu$ is reserved for the population mean.
:::
:::

::: {.se-score}
:::

## Dictionary {.se-theme-green}

Test yourself: say what each symbol means, then click **Reveal** to check.

::: {.se-dict-controls}
:::

### General notation

| Symbol | Meaning |
|:-------:|:-----------------------|
| $=$ | [equal to]{.se-flip} |
| $\neq$ | [not equal to]{.se-flip} |
| $\approx$ | [is approximately equal to]{.se-flip} |
| $\infty$ | [infinity]{.se-flip} |
| $\propto$ | [is proportional to]{.se-flip} |
| $\therefore$ | [therefore]{.se-flip} |
| $\because$ | [because]{.se-flip} |
| $<$ | [less than]{.se-flip} |
| $>$ | [greater than]{.se-flip} |
| $\le$ | [less than or equal to]{.se-flip} |
| $\ge$ | [greater than or equal to]{.se-flip} |
| $\implies$ | [implies]{.se-flip} |
| $:$ | [such that]{.se-flip} |
| $\forall$ | [for all]{.se-flip} |

### Set notation

| Symbol | Meaning |
|:-------:|:-----------------------|
| $\in$ | [is an element of]{.se-flip} |
| $\notin$ | [is not an element of]{.se-flip} |
| $\subset$ | [is a subset of]{.se-flip} |
| $\emptyset$ | [the empty set]{.se-flip} |
| $A'$ | [the complement of $A$]{.se-flip} |
| $\mathbb{N}$ | [the natural numbers]{.se-flip} |
| $\mathbb{Z}$ | [the integers]{.se-flip} |
| $\mathbb{R}$ | [the real numbers]{.se-flip} |
| $\mathbb{Q}$ | [the rational numbers]{.se-flip} |
| $\mathbb{C}$ | [the complex numbers]{.se-flip} |
| $\cup$ | [union]{.se-flip} |
| $\cap$ | [intersection]{.se-flip} |

### Series notation

| Symbol | Meaning |
|:-------:|:-----------------------|
| $\sum$ | [sum of]{.se-flip} |
| $\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i$ | [$a_1 + a_2 + \dots + a_n$]{.se-flip} |
| $\prod$ | [product of]{.se-flip} |
| $\prod_{i=1}^{n} a_i$ | [$a_1 \times a_2 \times \dots \times a_n$]{.se-flip} |
| $n!$ | [$n$ factorial $= n \times (n-1) \times \dots \times 2 \times 1$]{.se-flip} |
| $\binom{n}{k}$ | [$n$ choose $k$ (the binomial coefficient)]{.se-flip} |
| ${}^{n}C_{k}$ | [$n$ choose $k$ (the binomial coefficient)]{.se-flip} |

### Function notation

| Symbol | Meaning |
|:-------:|:-----------------------|
| $f: x \mapsto y$ | [the function $f$ maps $x$ onto $y$]{.se-flip} |
| $f^{-1}$ | [the inverse of $f$]{.se-flip} |
| $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to \infty} f(x)$ | [the limit of $f(x)$ as $x$ tends to infinity]{.se-flip} |

::: {.se-box}
**Remember:** choice of notation is often cultural or simply personal preference. If your lecturer uses something you don't recognise, it is okay to ask.
:::
